candidates.text:
Surprise 1: Anthropic acquired a one-person biotech
.
.
.
Surprise 2: that person is me
Surprise 3: I’m here to tell you all about it

Yes, this is what you think it is; after 6 yrs of increasingly loose anonymity: the Professor Oak reveal post

…and yes, it has gotten so boring around here that I’m literally doxxing myself to spice up the timeline

-------
Ok, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Cody Tranbarger. I mostly tweet, but occasionally find time to dabble in drug dev & starting/building biotechs. My past lives span the VC, crossover, startup continuum; Prof Oak has been my way of keeping a digital foot in those worlds, despite having my physical feet planted elsewhere.

The past 18 mo, ‘elsewhere’ was Mithril Medicine, a co. I founded to develop bsAbs for LAMA2-CMD & other ECM-related genetic diseases.

Mithril was born out of hands-on building with @MikeNGladstone, @JasonPaulRhodes, @LifeSciVC, & team @atlasventure. Somehow, I made enough half-decent calls along the way (even a broken clock is right twice a day, eh?) to convince them Mithril/I warranted a small seed. While I can hardly rationalize such an outrageously cavalier bet, I’m grateful for it, & I'd partner with Atlas again in a heartbeat.

In typical AV fashion, Mithril’s primordial form was virtual, decentralized, & ultra-lean. This stage tends to be short-lived, but for Mithril, it worked surprisingly well, for surprisingly long, thanks in part to the rapid maturation of the AI tools I used liberally.

Eventually, Mithril became a bit of an experiment itself - to find the upper bound of how far it could scale as a single operator + a bunch of Claude (+ a stellar bench of part-time consultants).

In parallel, I started spending time with @nc_frey, @an1lam, & @CoefficientBio team; and promptly experienced, for the 1st time, AI at the frontier. Soon thereafter, Mithril stopped looking like an experiment, & started looking like a preview of an entirely new operating model.

From that spark came “Pipeline-in-a-Person.” The idea immediately resonated when we shared it here back in April; and it was central to the shared vision that led to Anthropic’s acquisition of Mithril, & my joining the team.

Why join Anthropic? Three reasons.
(1) For Mithril, the programs continue, with more resources & infrastructure behind them, and as much Claude as I can put to work.

(2) For me, the chance to start several more programs, & find out how many one person can actually run in parallel - an almost unprecedented luxury for a curious drug hunter.

(3) For our mission, a path to institutionalize & scale this new way of working, then put it in the hands of all of biopharma, all over the world - which, candidly, I find the most energizing.

Will AI x Bio cure diseases? Unequivocally yes, imo… but not by the route that gets the most airtime. Rather than timeline acceleration & compression, I see orchestration & parallelization as today's low-hanging fruit.

Most drug hunters see a handful of go/no-go calls in a career, & spend entirely too much of the rest trading emails (my inbox can attest).

Give them the bandwidth to run several programs at once, and the time to focus on scientific judgment, and I’m willing to bet they’ll make better calls. And at scale, better calls translate to more drugs, higher hit rates, broader patient impact, & likely, a disease or 10 or 100 cured. I couldn't be more excited to build toward that future @AnthropicAI.

Finally, a heartfelt thank you to BioTwitter/X. The end of anonymity is bittersweet, but if anyone’s earned a proper introduction, you all have.

It’s difficult to overstate how much this app has done for me: a decade of education, plenty of friends, many job opportunities, several mentors, a few investors, even a co-founder (fmr). It was the generosity of this community that inspired me to start posting 6 years ago, after just as many years lurking. I hope I’ve been able to pay it forward, in my own small way.

But, to be clear, Prof Oak isn’t going anywhere. Same beat, same themes, and now, a front-row seat to drug development at the frontier. Stay tuned for dispatches from the trenches; and remember...

Gotta Cure 'Em All

candidates.text:
almost a decade+ ago while working in big tech i changed my visible title to "applied generalist" because this is basically how i thought about myself from the moment i was on the internet as a kid. i didn't jive with product management cuz i wasn't supposed to write code (ppl would look at you weirdly if you did this), & i hated the idea of being just an engineer because ppl would just treat you like a code monkey, & i hated being in design because ppl often just treated you as a pixel pusher.

legacy companies (which i now include big tech as part of) are still organized around highly specific roles like these + levels, & career ladders. i.e. your position in the hierarchy determines not only what you actually do but also how ppl interact with you.

i remember walking into meetings with VPs who didn't know how to treat me cuz they couldn't place me in a ladder due to my lack of an officially sanctioned title. & i absolutely hated this existence with a passion. being pigeonholed into a narrowly defined function felt like wearing a kind of straitjacket. 

this is why the member of technical staff movement with ai companies is so damn necessary. if you as a company do not move towards a more general model like this, you will absolutely get left behind & alienate ppl who can perform across the spectrum.

candidates.text:
Chris asked a fair question about upgrade logic. 

The logic is pretty simple: the longer someone has had their robot, the more wear and tear it has, and the more work it takes for us to bring it up to Serene performance — reducing noise while keeping cleaning efficacy exactly the same. This is atoms and any HW that's used for more than year will require far more rigorous testing and upgrade than HW that is a month old.  

Candidly, We considered offering one flat upgrade price, but it just wasn’t feasible. As we’ve mentioned before, Matic may look the same on the outside, but internally we’ve made many changes over time to improve quality and reliability. On older robots, bringing them up to Serene performance can mean replacing the entire vacuum stack along with many other components affected by wear.  

Customers who’ve had their Matic serviced before have probably seen this firsthand. We often upgrade parts they didn’t even ask about, and for many early adopters we did that at no charge when we were addressing reliability issues.   

That’s really the reason the upgrade cost varies with the age of the robot.

candidates.text:
Anthropic’s S1 Breakdown

Overall, fairly solid all things considered:

1) ~10,000ish customers paying $100K per year. 

That’s nothing, much more room to grow. 

2) Cash levels are strong, and Anthropic has more cash than most public companies. 

3) Capex obligations are less than OpenAI

4) Anthropic’s spend on R&D is nearly 60% of Revenue. 

If they cut that to 50% they would be breakeven. (They have levers.)

5) Anthropic is getting financing from its suppliers and Blackstone and bank syndicate groups. 

6) Anthropic’s ‘losses’ are due to accounting around the converible note

So, Anthropic has access to financing both from its own operations and well capitalized third parties. 

I am interviewing @MParekh about Anthropic’s S1 and what it means this week!

What I don’t like:

1) Hard to see training and inference breakout

2) Top customer concentration is massive. And those players can roll out their own coding tools and are working on that too. 

Anthropic needs to maintain the best technical edge so it customers don’t become competitors. 

3) Switching costs are low.

candidates.text:
Yes, I learnt this lesson a little late in life. Not because I was afraid, but because I was not convinced, or rather not confident, that I could change anything.

I know there are millions of people like me who mean well and who care about freedom and the misuse and abuse of government power.

But most of us have been taught to believe that the answer is to give the government more power and elect good and honest people to run it. It hardly ever works as intended, because power attracts power-hungry people, and they care most about holding on to that power, even if it means wrecking whole societies.

I now believe the actual, practical solution is to keep very little in the hands of the government and let people freely compete and cooperate with each other. That, to me, is the most moral system there is. And it is worth speaking up for, come what may.
